# defining custom object to store hyperparameter configs and error rate outputs 
class ffObject(object):

    def __init__(self, experiment_type, epochs, hidden_nodes, hidden_layers,
                 init_mode, learning_rate, dropout, act_type, model=None):

        self.experiment_type = experiment_type
        self.epochs = epochs
        self.hidden_nodes = hidden_nodes
        self.hidden_layers = hidden_layers
        self.init_mode = init_mode
        self.learning_rate = learning_rate
        self.dropout = dropout
        self.act_type = act_type
        self.model = model

        self.train_error = 0.0
        self.validation_error = 0.0
        self.test_error = 0.0

        self.train_f1_measure = 0.0
        self.validation_f1_measure = 0.0
        self.test_f1_measure = 0.0

        self.execution_time = 0.0

        self.training_error_epoch = []
        self.validation_error_epoch = []
        self.testing_error_epoch = []
        self.epoch_times = []


def make_ffObject(experiment_type, epochs, hidden_nodes,
                  hidden_layers, init_mode, learning_rate, dropout, act_type):
    
    return ffObject(experiment_type, epochs, hidden_nodes,
                    hidden_layers, init_mode, learning_rate, dropout, act_type)

# Need a training dataset, a validation dataset and a testing data set for the following reasons: 
# Training set: is used to learn the patterns 
#   - this is the set that is used to fit the machine learning model, where the algorithm learns patterns, relationships, and parameters 
# Validation set: is used to tune and optimize the model 
#   - separate subset of data used to tune model hyperparameters and make design decisions during training. Provides an unbiased estimate of model performance during development
# Testing set: is used to measure the final performance and generalization 
#   - Completely independent subset used to evaluate the final model's performance after all training and tuning are complete. Simulates how the model will perform on unseen, real-world data and provides the most reliable estimate of generalization.  


train_loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(dataset=training_dataset, batch_size=batch_size, shuffle=True)

# Neural Network class using sigmoid --> contains the hidden layer as forward

class NeuralNet(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_size, hidden_size, num_classes, hidden_layers, dropout, act_type):
        super(NeuralNet, self).__init__()

        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(p=dropout)

        if act_type == "sigmoid": 
            self.activation_type = nn.Sigmoid()  # defined as: f(x) = 1 / (1 + e^-x)
        elif act_type == "relu":
            self.activation_type = nn.ReLU() # defined as: f(x)=max(0,x)
        
        self.hidden_layers_count = hidden_layers

        # makes the hidden layer count visible to all modules methods (ie; forward)
        # more info can be found in pytorch docs here:
        #  https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.Module.html#torch.nn.Module
        # https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.ModuleList.html

        self.hidden_layers = nn.ModuleList()
        # self.layer = nn.Linear(input_size, hidden_size)


        self.hidden_layers.append(nn.Linear(input_size, hidden_size))

        for i in range(hidden_layers - 1 ):
            self.hidden_layers.append(nn.Linear(hidden_size, hidden_size))

        self.output = nn.Linear(hidden_size, num_classes)

    # this is the hidden layer and it is set to one as: input layer -> hidden layer : forward[l1 -> sigmoid -> l2] -> output layer
    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.dropout(x)
        out = x 

        for layer in self.hidden_layers:
            out = layer(out)
            out = self.activation_type(out)
        # out = self.layer(x) # layer one, gets x value 
        # out = self.sigmoid(out) # takes previous output and outputs new value: 
        
        
        # Sigmoid function outputs in the range (0, 1), it is ideal to use for binary classification problems 
        # works well for finding the probability of the data belonging to a particular class
        # can learn more about the sigmoid function here: https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/python/python-tensorflow-nn-sigmoid/
        out = self.output(out) # layer two, takes output from sigmoid 
        return out

# used to initialize weights by type 
def init_weights_bias(model, mode="random"):
    for layer in model.modules():
        if isinstance(layer, nn.Linear):
            if mode == "random-xavier":
                # need to init the weights here to random small value from a uniform distribution
                # bias can be set to zero 
                # reasoning behind using this for sigmid: https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/deep-learning/xavier-initialization/
                nn.init.xavier_uniform_(layer.weight)
                nn.init.zeros_(layer.bias)
            elif mode == "random-kaiming":
                # using xavier uniform for relu due to the vanishing or exploding gradient problem 
                # can learn more by checking out: https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/deep-learning/kaiming-initialization-in-deep-learning/
                nn.init.kaiming_uniform_(layer.weight)
                nn.init.zeros_(layer.bias)
            elif mode == "zero":
                nn.init.zeros_(layer.weight)
                nn.init.zeros_(layer.bias)

In [138]:
def evaluate_error_and_f1(model, loader, device):
    model.eval()
    n_correct = 0
    n_samples = 0

    all_labels = []
    all_predication = []
    with torch.no_grad():
        for images, labels, in loader:
            images = images.reshape(images.size(0), -1).to(device)
            labels = labels.to(device)

            outputs = model(images)
            _, predictions = torch.max(outputs, 1)

            n_samples += labels.shape[0]
            n_correct += (predictions == labels).sum().item()

            all_labels.extend(labels.cpu().numpy())
            all_predication.extend(predictions.cpu().numpy())

    error = 1 - (n_correct / n_samples)
    f1 = f1_score(all_labels, all_predication, average="macro")
    
    return error, f1

In [139]:
# step a) batch size set to 250 --> rest of hyperparameters set to predetermined values 
# this is basically the baseline used for all other steps and will use these hyperparameters for each step besides the ones that need to modifying 


input_size = 3072
batch_size = 250
num_classes = 10


# baseline_setup = make_ffObject(experiment_type="baseline", epochs=4, hidden_nodes=150, hidden_layers=1, init_mode="zero", learning_rate=0.25)

def run_experiment(setupObj):
    model = NeuralNet(input_size, setupObj.hidden_nodes, num_classes, setupObj.hidden_layers, setupObj.dropout, setupObj.act_type).to(device)
    init_weights_bias(model, setupObj.init_mode)

    # loss and optimizer
    criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
    optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=setupObj.learning_rate)

    start_time = time.time()
    for epoch in range(setupObj.epochs):
        model.train()

        for images, labels in train_loader:
            
            # need to reshape data properly  
            images = images.reshape(images.size(0), -1).to(device)
            labels = labels.to(device)

            # forward pass 
            outputs = model(images)
            loss = criterion(outputs, labels) 

            # backwards pass
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            loss.backward()
            optimizer.step()


    setupObj.execution_time = time.time() - start_time

    setupObj.train_error, setupObj.train_f1_measure = evaluate_error_and_f1(model, train_loader, device)
    setupObj.validation_error, setupObj.validation_f1_measure = evaluate_error_and_f1(model, validation_loader, device)

    setupObj.model = model

    return setupObj

Analysis for Each Step:

Step A: Analysis

In [147]:
baseline_results = pd.DataFrame({
    "Epochs": [baseline_setup.epochs],
    "Training Error Rate": [baseline_setup.train_error],
    "Validation Error Rate": [baseline_setup.validation_error],
    "Testing Error Rate": [baseline_setup.test_error]
})

print(baseline_results)

   Epochs  Training Error Rate  Validation Error Rate  Testing Error Rate
0       6             0.549067                 0.5688              0.5688

This was the baseline configuration set up I used to create a stable comparable batch that could be used across the board, where I can change hyperparameters in later experiments one at a time. The baseline used the following parameters:

  • epochs: 6
  • hidden nodes: 150
  • hidden layers: 1
  • initialization mode: xavier uniform
  • learning rate: 0.15
  • drop out: 0
  • activation type: sigmoid

This baseline produced training error of roughly 0.8079 and validation error of roughly 0.8068 and a testing error rate of 0.807. The errors rates are extremely close together and nearly identical which is a strong indicator that overfitting has not occurred, however it is very likely that this model is underfiting. The model is underfitting and is failing to fully learn important patterns, which can happen due to the model being to simple, regularization is to high, features are weak or missing, not enough training, along with a couple other possibilities. CIFAR-10 is too complex for a fully connected network as o feed multi-dimensional data into a nn layer flattening is required. This involves removing rich data from an image, it distorts and destroys the spatial relationship between the data points, however through the flattening process the image is now in a format that can be passed to the model correctly. Sigmoid can also slow down the learning due to vanishing gradients. The I also choose to use the xavier uniform for initialization as it helps prevent the vanishing or exploding gradients which can occur if the variance changes drastically between layer.

This baseline is used for relative comparison across varying hyperparameters in the following steps.

Before diving into the analysis, a quick introduction on epochs will help provide relevant context to understand what is being evaluated. An epoch represent a single full pass through the entire training dataset. By increasing the number of epochs it allows the network to to update the weights multiple times, and hopefully reducing the training error rates.

By increasing the it generally improves the accuracy initially as the model has more opportunities to learn the patterns in the data. However it is possible to hit a certain problem where each additional epoch contributes to overfitting, which is when a model memorizes the training data instead of generalizing it. This experiment showcases both the gradual decrease in training and validation error rates as well as the problem with overfitting. The epochs between 2 to 6 show a gradual decline over time, where it spikes up again when there are 8 epochs showing overfitting. However when you look beyond this to epoch 10 you can observe tha it hits similar error rates as when epochs are set at 8, showcasing that even though the model started improving again it was not significant enough to be worth the tradeoff in training time.

Through this observation it is evident that training longer (more epochs) helps to improve training data but once the model has made us of the useful information and structure the validation performance stabilizes. Therefore increasing epochs leads to increase performance and accuracy but only up until a certain point, where improvements past that become uncertain due to potential issues such as overfitting and not being worth the tradeoff.

As I did earlier, before diving into the analysis a quick discussion on what hidden nodes are will help with further understanding. The number of hidden nodes helps represent the features of a feedforward neural network. A hidden layer (which will be discussed further in the relevant section) transforms the inputs into more complex feature representation. By increasing the number of neurons it also increases the number of weights, which allows the network to model more complex patterns.

This experiment showcases that increasing the hidden nodes from 2 to 113 significantly reduces both training and validation error rates. The network underfits with only two hidden nodes as it lacks enough power to capture the structure of the data. The lowest error rates occur at 113 hidden nodes with leads us to the most optimal value as it is the perfect balance between the models capacity and generalization.

Once we look past 113 hidden nodes we can see a gradual increase in error rates again suggesting that the model may becoming overtly complex in comparison to its dataset. This leads to optimization struggling and reduces performance, and increase the hidden nodes also increases internal dimensionality which can impact learning efficiency as well.

Overall this experiment showed that there is a balance that should be met, where to few nodes lead to underfitting and to many can negatively impact performance.

Weight initialization is used to determine the starting values of the network parameters, and since neural networks learn by adjusting weights through gradient descent as having poor initialization can prevent effective learning.

In this experiment when using xavier initialization the training and validation error rates were roughly 0.85 and in comparison when set to zero the error rates were around 0.90. When set to zero all hidden nodes (neurons) start with identical weights which cause them to learn the same features and limits the network.

Why I used xavier_uniform over simple_uniform for initialization

  • Simple uniform initialization selects weights from a fixed range. It does not consider the layer size, which can lead to vanishing or exploding gradients which is a big problem
  • Xavier uniform initialization scales the weights effectively. It is based on the number of input and output hidden nodes (neurons), which helps to maintain stable activation across all layers. Overall improving gradient flow leading to more stable training.

The learning rate is a key hyperparameter that is used to control how large each step is when updating weights during training. According to IBM, the learning rate determines how much a model's parameter changes within the optimization step. It also affects how well a model learns and if it can learn without making overtly large corrections. A low learning rate leads to small updates, whereas a high learning rate can cause the training process to overshoot and become unstable.

It is also discussed that (geeksforgeeks) that the learning rate affects both convergence speed and model performance.

  • low learning rate leads to slow convergence
  • high learning rate can speed up training but risks making unstable updates
  • an optimal learning rate balances speed and stability

Within the experiment, very small learning rates ranging from 0.0005 to 0.05 produced high error rates that was close to 0.90. This indicates that the weight updates were to small to make any meaningful progress within the alloted epochs. The performance saw a gradual then sharp decrease in error rates between 0.05 to 0.1, where the experiment reached its optimal result of roughly 0.8165 validation error. This indicates that this value allows the model to make large and stable enough updates to minimize loss. There is a slight improvement when looking at the learning rate of 0.5 for training but the testing error rate increase here, it become clear that it is not worth the tradeoff.

Overall, the results obtained from the experiment showcase that the best learning rate balances both convergence speed and training stability.

The hidden layer is one or more layers placed between the input and output layers. Each of these layers are responsible fro learning the complex patterns within the dataset. Each neuron (hidden node) within a hidden layer applies a weighted sum of inputs followed by a non-linear activation function (GeeksForGeeks). Based off this information it should be obvious that increasing the layers within a model should increase the expressive power.

However as we can clearly see within the graph, that is not the case here. Where only having one hidden layer results in the best training and validation error rate of roughly 0.787 while adding more layers rapidly increases the error rate until it stabilizes roughly around 0.9.

As noted in stanford's cs231 notes, deeper networks are harder to train. This can be due to optimization challenges regarding vanishing gradients where when using sigmoid activation, when a gradient is almost 0 it effectively kills the gradient which means almost no signal will flow through the neurons to the weights. It also becomes an issue of complexity, as realistically more layers should be better, but it becomes much more complex. By simply adding layers it increases the parameter count and makes gradient decent harder, without introducing complexity.

Overall based on my implementation and minimal complexity one hidden layer is sufficient and provides the optimal training error rate. Whereas more layers lead to to training difficulties and decreases performance.

sources: https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/deep-learning/feedforward-neural-network/ https://cs231n.github.io/neural-networks-1/# --> from stanford

Dropout is a regularization technique that randomly selects and sets a fraction of the neuron outputs to zero during training (GeeksForGeeks). The dropout rate represents the proportion of neurons that are removed at each training step, through this is becomes possible to reduce reliance on activations and helps to improve generalization. Within the notes of sc231 by stanford, it explains that dropout introduces stochastic behaviour during training and is commonly tuned using the validation performance metrics.

Within my experiment it can be seen that increasing the dropout rate from 0.2 to 0.3 reduces both the test and validation error rate proving that a dropout rate of 0.2 was not enough. At 0.3 the model most likely achieved a better balance between learning and preventing overfitting.

At 0.4 the error rate rose again slightly, which could mean that there were to many neurons being removed affecting the models effective capacity. At 0.5 the model improved again slightly which when tying back into cs231 it aligns with their discussion that dropout is extremely effective bust should be validated.

Overall the results shown help to argue that dropout helps improve generalization, and that having to little may cause overfitting and to much may reduce learning efficiency.

input_size = 3072
batch_size = 250
num_classes = 10


# baseline_setup = make_ffObject(experiment_type="baseline", epochs=4, hidden_nodes=150, hidden_layers=1, init_mode="zero", learning_rate=0.25)

def run_experiment_loaders(setupObj, train_loader_iter, validation_loader_iter, device):
    
    setupObj.training_error_epoch = []
    setupObj.validation_error_epoch = []
    model = NeuralNet(input_size, setupObj.hidden_nodes, num_classes, setupObj.hidden_layers, setupObj.dropout, setupObj.act_type).to(device)
    init_weights_bias(model, setupObj.init_mode)

    # loss and optimizer
    criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
    optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=setupObj.learning_rate)

    n_total_steps = len(train_loader_iter)
    start_time = 0
    start_time = time.time()
    for epoch in range(setupObj.epochs):
        model.train()
        optimizer.zero_grad()  #update weights once per epoch using gradients from entire dataset 

        for images, labels in train_loader_iter:
            
            # need to reshape data properly  
            images = images.reshape(images.size(0), -1).to(device)
            labels = labels.to(device)

            # forward pass 
            outputs = model(images)
            loss = criterion(outputs, labels) 

            # backwards pass
            loss.backward()

        # step
        optimizer.step() # for true BGD only one optimizer step per epoch

    setupObj.execution_time = time.time() - start_time

    
    setupObj.train_error, setupObj.train_f1_measure = evaluate_error_and_f1(model, train_loader_iter, device)
    setupObj.validation_error, setupObj.validation_f1_measure = evaluate_error_and_f1(model, validation_loader_iter, device)
    
    setupObj.model = model

    return setupObj

                fold_validation_f1_measure.append(run_setup.validation_f1_measure)

                fold_test_errors.append(test_error)
                fold_test_f1_measure.append(test_f1)

                fold_training_times.append(run_setup.execution_time)

                # print("\nTrain error: ", fold_train_errors)
                # print("V error: ", fold_validation_errors)
                # print("Train F1: ", fold_train_f1_measure)
                # print("V F1: ", fold_validation_f1_measure)

                # print("Test error: ", test_error)
                # print("Test F1: ", test_f1)

                # print("Training Time: ", fold_training_times)




            mean_train_error = np.mean(fold_train_errors)
            mean_validation_error = np.mean(fold_validation_errors)

            mean_train_f1_measure = np.mean(fold_train_f1_measure)
            mean_validation_f1_measure = np.mean(fold_validation_f1_measure)

            mean_test_error = np.mean(fold_test_errors)
            mean_test_f1_measure = np.mean(fold_test_f1_measure)

            mean_training_time = np.mean(fold_training_times)

            single_pass_results = {
                "lr": lr, "nodes": hn, "epochs": e, 
                "Train Error": mean_train_error, "Validation Error": mean_validation_error, "Testing Error": mean_test_error,
                "Train F1 Measure": mean_train_f1_measure, "Validation F1 Measure": mean_validation_f1_measure, "Testing F1 Measure": mean_test_f1_measure,
                "Training Time": mean_training_time
            }

            all_results.append(single_pass_results)

            if mean_validation_error < best_validation_error:
                best_validation_error = mean_validation_error
                best_setup = single_pass_results

            # print(single_pass_results)

            # print(f"LR: {lr} | Nodes: {hn} | Epochs: {e} | Val Error: {mean_validation_error:.4f}")

Part 4: CNN

CNN architecture looks like

conv relu conv relu pool

conv relu conv relu pool

conv relu conv relu pool

convolution layer: image + filter = resulting image --> usually results in smaller output image

max pooling layer: apply filter to subregions --> take max of each region (used to reduce number of params and avoid overfitting)

# defining custom object to store hyperparameter configs and error rate outputs 
class cnnObject(object):
    def __init__(self, experiment_type, epochs, learning_rate, fc_layers,
                 fc_width=120, dropout=0.0, model=None):

        self.experiment_type = experiment_type
        self.epochs = epochs
        self.learning_rate = learning_rate

        # Grid search variables
        self.fc_layers = fc_layers
        self.fc_width = fc_width
        self.dropout = dropout

        # Outputs
        self.model = model
        self.execution_time = 0.0

        self.train_error = 0.0
        self.train_f1_measure = 0.0

        self.validation_error = 0.0
        self.validation_f1_measure = 0.0

        self.test_error = 0.0
        self.test_f1_measure = 0.0


def make_cnn_object(experiment_type, epochs, learning_rate, fc_layers,
                 fc_width=120, dropout=0.0):
    return cnnObject(experiment_type, epochs, learning_rate, fc_layers, fc_width, dropout)
In [199]:
class CNN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_classes=10, fc_width=120, fc_layers=2, dropout=0.0):
        super(CNN, self).__init__()

        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(p=dropout)
        self.activation  = nn.ReLU()

        self.fc_layers_count = fc_layers

        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(3, 6, 5) # 3 colour 
        self.pool = nn.MaxPool2d(2, 2)  # 2x2
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(6, 16, 5)  #input must be size of last output: ie 6 output --> 6 input

        self.flattend_feature_size = 16*5*5

        self.fc_hidden_layers = nn.ModuleList()

        if fc_layers > 1:

            # this will create the first hidden layer 
            self.fc_hidden_layers.append(nn.Linear(self.flattend_feature_size, fc_width))

            # create additional layers 
            for i in range(fc_layers - 2):
                self.fc_hidden_layers.append(nn.Linear(fc_width, fc_width))

            self.output = nn.Linear(fc_width, num_classes)

        else: 
            self.output = nn.Linear(self.flattend_feature_size, num_classes)

        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(16*5*5, 120)  # 16*5*5 is fixed 
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(120, 84)
        self.fc3 = nn.Linear(84, 10)  # 10 is fixed here 

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.pool(F.relu(self.conv1(x)))  # first convo and pooling layer
        x = self.pool(F.relu(self.conv2(x)))  # second convo and pooling layer
        x = x.view(x.size(0), -1)  # flatten near end 

        out = self.dropout(x)

        for layer in self.fc_hidden_layers:
            out = layer(out)
            out = self.activation(out)
            out = self.dropout(out)

        out = self.output(out)
        return out

def cnn_evaluate_error_and_f1(model, loader, device):
    model.eval()
    n_correct = 0
    n_samples = 0

    all_labels = []
    all_predication = []
    with torch.no_grad():
        for images, labels, in loader:
            images = images.to(device)
            labels = labels.to(device)

            outputs = model(images)
            _, predictions = torch.max(outputs, 1)

            n_samples += labels.shape[0]
            n_correct += (predictions == labels).sum().item()

            all_labels.extend(labels.cpu().numpy())
            all_predication.extend(predictions.cpu().numpy())

    error = 1 - (n_correct / n_samples)
    f1 = float(f1_score(all_labels, all_predication, average="macro"))
    
    return error, f1

def run_cnn_experiment(setupObj):
    model = CNN(num_classes=10, fc_width=setupObj.fc_width, fc_layers=setupObj.fc_layers, dropout=setupObj.dropout).to(device)

    criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
    optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=setupObj.learning_rate, momentum=0.9)

    start_time = time.time()
    for epoch in range(setupObj.epochs):
        model.train()

        for images, labels in train_loader: 
            images = images.to(device) 
            labels = labels.to(device)

            # forward pass
            outputs = model(images)
            loss = criterion(outputs, labels)

            # backwards and optimize 
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            loss.backward()
            optimizer.step()

    setupObj.execution_time = time.time() - start_time

    setupObj.train_error, setupObj.train_f1_measure = cnn_evaluate_error_and_f1(model, train_loader, device)
    setupObj.validation_error, setupObj.validation_f1_measure = cnn_evaluate_error_and_f1(model, validation_loader, device)

    setupObj.model = model

    return setupObj

            print(f"Starting configuration {count}")

            setup = make_cnn_object(

    plt.xticks(sorted(df["fc_layers"].unique()))
    plt.legend()
    plt.grid(True)
    plt.show()
